title: India's Oil Import Bill Surges as Iran War Sends Crude Prices Past $90
excerpt: Brent crude hit a five-week high of $90.75 per barrel on Monday as renewed fighting choked the Strait of Hormuz, piling fresh pressure on India's already ballooning energy import costs and weakening rupee.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's oil import bill surged 82% year-on-year to $18.7 billion in May.
  • Brent crude reached $90.75 per barrel, a five-week high, amid Middle East tensions.
  • The Indian rupee fell to a two-month low of 96.5250 per dollar.
  • Russia supplied over 53% of India's crude imports in June, totaling 2.7 million barrels per day.

  • India's energy import bill jumped 82% year-on-year in May to $18.7 billion as Hormuz disruptions forced costlier supply routes
  • Brent crude spiked to $90.75 per barrel on Monday — a five-week high — before easing to around $88 after Iran hinted at possible negotiations
  • The Indian rupee hit a two-month low of 96.5250 per dollar, with the RBI intervening through state-run banks to stem losses
  • Russia accounted for over 53% of India's crude imports in June, with record purchases of 2.7 million barrels per day

Hormuz Chokepoint Tightens Again

India's crude oil import bill is climbing at its steepest rate in years, with the escalating U.S.-Iran conflict driving Brent crude past $90 per barrel on Monday and threatening to widen the country's already swollen trade deficit further.

Brent crude surged to an intraday high of $90.75 — its highest level in five weeks — before pulling back to around $88.26 after Iran's foreign ministry signalled that negotiations with the United States "could be pursued based on national interests," according to Reuters. West Texas Intermediate also retreated to $82.18 after briefly trading above $83.

The latest price spike was triggered by the near-total shutdown of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Just four vessels made the transit on Sunday, down from eight the day before, according to LSEG data. The U.S. conducted its ninth consecutive day of military strikes against Iran, while Tehran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two oil tankers attempting to cross the waterway were struck and immobilized after detonating in an Iranian minefield.

"The anticipated recovery in shipping has effectively stalled."

— ANZ Analysts, Research Note

A Ballooning Energy Bill

"India's CPI surged to 4.38% in June — the highest since December 2024 and above the RBI's 4% midpoint target."

India, the world's third-largest oil importer, is bearing the brunt of the crisis. The country paid $18.7 billion on oil and gas imports in May alone — an 81.6% increase from the $10.3 billion it spent in May 2025, according to provisional data from India's oil ministry reported by OilPrice.com. In April, the oil import bill reached $18.6 billion against an average of $13 billion during the previous quarter, driven by the Indian crude basket averaging $114 per barrel.

The shock is now feeding into consumer prices. India's CPI surged to 4.38% in June — the highest since December 2024 and above the RBI's 4% midpoint target. Food inflation accelerated to 5.32%, while the wholesale price index hit an all-time high of 9.87%, driven by mineral oils, food, and base metals.

The widening trade deficit, which expanded to $28.4 billion in April from $20.7 billion in March, has started to pressure the government's current account and public finances. Estimates suggest each $1-per-barrel increase sustained over a year adds roughly ₹16,000 crore to India's annual import bill.

Russia Fills the Gulf Vacuum

With more than 40% of India's pre-war crude flows — those routed through the Strait of Hormuz — effectively cut off since late February, Indian refiners have turned overwhelmingly to Russian oil. India imported a record 2.7 million barrels per day of Russian crude in June, accounting for over 53% of total imports, according to data from Kpler cited by The Hindu BusinessLine.

Russian crude purchases totalled €4.5 billion ($5.14 billion) in June, a 32% increase month-on-month and 25% year-on-year, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). The Jamnagar refinery alone saw a 150% month-on-month surge in Russian crude arrivals.

"Russian crude imports rose to around 2.6 million bpd in June, accounting for more than 50% of India's crude imports, and have been steadily increasing since March."

— Sumit Ritolia, Lead Research Analyst, Kpler

India also increased purchases from Venezuela (300,000–400,000 bpd), Brazil, and West Africa. Total crude imports hit a record 5 million bpd in June, pushing crude oil inventories to 104 million barrels — recovering toward the pre-war level of 107 million barrels held at the end of February.

Rupee Under Pressure, Rate Hikes Loom

The currency markets have not been spared. The Indian rupee fell to 96.5250 per dollar on Monday — its weakest level since mid-May — before the Reserve Bank of India intervened through dollar sales via state-run banks. The currency settled at 96.4450, down nearly 0.2% on the day, according to Reuters.

Analysts at ING warned that elevated energy prices would keep the U.S. Federal Reserve alert, limiting dollar weakness globally. Swap markets in India are pricing in about 70 basis points of RBI rate hikes over the next 12 months — a sharp reversal from the easing cycle many had expected before the war.

The combination of rising inflation, a swelling trade deficit, and a weakening currency has materially narrowed the RBI's room to manoeuvre at its August monetary policy meeting.

What Comes Next

The collapse of the June ceasefire — with President Trump declaring it "over" at the NATO summit in Ankara — has dashed hopes of a quick return to normal Hormuz shipping. Gulf countries had briefly boosted crude and condensate exports to their highest levels since before the war in early July, but flows are now slowing again.

For Indian consumers, the pain is already arriving. Fuel price hikes last month, mirroring elevated crude costs, have begun straining trucking and logistics industries. Goldman Sachs estimates that pipeline projects in the Middle East could eventually carry about 60% of the oil currently shipped through Hormuz by the end of 2028 — but that is cold comfort for an economy paying the price today.

Iran has also threatened to press Houthi allies to close the Red Sea route if the U.S. attacks Iranian power infrastructure, raising the spectre of further disruption. For Indian households sending money home and NRIs watching their rupee-denominated savings erode, the oil shock is no longer a distant geopolitical event — it is showing up in grocery bills and remittance values alike.
